q: The commonest cause of neonatal sepsis and meningitis in the first week is:
e: Group B streptococcus, followed by E. coli and Listeria, causes early-onset disease.

q: A risk factor for early-onset neonatal sepsis is:
o: Rupture of the membranes for more than 18 hours
e: Prolonged rupture of the membranes, maternal fever and maternal group B streptococcus raise the risk.

q: The first-line antibiotics for neonatal sepsis are:
e: WHO 2024: ampicillin and gentamicin for at least 10 days.

q: Why is ampicillin added for neonatal meningitis?
o: To cover group B streptococcus only

q: Which antibiotic should be avoided in a jaundiced newborn?
e: Ceftriaxone displaces bilirubin from albumin and precipitates with calcium.
Cytomegalovirus: 90% of infected babies have no signs at birth, and it is the commonest infectious cause of deafness.

q: Cataract, sensorineural deafness and a patent ductus arteriosus in a newborn suggest:
e: This is the classic triad of congenital rubella.

q: Hydrocephalus, chorioretinitis and diffuse intracranial calcification suggest:
e: This is congenital toxoplasmosis. Cytomegalovirus causes periventricular calcification.

q: A 7-day-old baby delivered at home stopped sucking and has spasms when touched; he is alert. What is the diagnosis?
e: Trismus and spasms after unclean cord care, in the baby of an unvaccinated mother, indicate neonatal tetanus.

q: A 3-day-old has heavy purulent discharge from the eyes and swollen eyelids. What is the treatment?
e: Gonococcal ophthalmia (days 2–5) can perforate the cornea and needs systemic ceftriaxone.
